discovery: Invention and realization of the optical lattice atomic clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping thousands of neutral atoms at a 'magic wavelength' where the lattice light leaves the clock transition unperturbed, and demonstrated it with strontium. Ye turned this concept into the most accurate and stable clocks ever built, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and below, resolving gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample, and pioneering many-body and spin-squeezed clock operation. Together their work has improved timekeeping by two orders of magnitude beyond caesium standards, motivates the redefinition of the SI second, and has created a new instrument for fundamental physics: searches for variations of fundamental constants and dark matter, tests of general relativity and relativistic geodesy. As someone who measures masses and magnetic moments with single trapped ions, I regard this as the defining achievement of precision physics of the past two decades: ingenious instrumentation that opens a genuine route to discovery.
